summary: Defines a DHCP option that passes a domain search list from the server to the client, which the client uses when resolving hostnames with DNS. This lets a short name be tried against several domains.

eli5.summary: If you type a short name, the computer needs to know which neighborhoods to look in. This option lets the network hand it that list.

questions: what is the dhcp domain search option
how does dhcp set the dns search list
how are search domains encoded in dhcp
what is a dns search list
subtitle: How a DHCP server hands a client the list of domains to try when it looks up a short hostname.

tldr.problem: A DHCP client can be told its DNS servers, but not which domains to append when a user types a short name like myhost.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCP option, code 119, carries a search list of domain names from the server to the client, packed with DNS name compression to save space.
tldr.outcome: Clients can be configured with a domain search list for DNS lookups. The RFC warns that a rogue DHCP server could abuse the option to redirect traffic.

today: RFC 3397 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so this RFC remains the definition of DHCP option 119.

sections.title: Why a Search List Option
sections.content:
DHCP (RFC 2131) lets a server give a client its configuration. RFC 2132 and RFC 2937 already let servers pass name service settings to clients. This RFC adds one more: the domain search list used when resolving hostnames with DNS.

The option applies only to DNS. It does not apply to other name resolution mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Your computer can already be told who to ask for addresses. This adds a list of places to look when you only give half a name.

sections.title: The Domain Search Option
sections.content:
The option code is 119. After the code comes a length byte and then the Searchstring data, which holds the search list.

One option can carry at most 255 octets. If the list is longer, multiple options MAY be used, as described in RFC 3396. In that case the data parts of all the Domain Search Options are concatenated into one block before the client interprets them.
sections.eli5: The option is a labeled envelope with a number on it, a size, and the list inside. A long list can be split across several envelopes.

sections.title: Compact Encoding of Names
sections.content:
The search strings MUST be concatenated and encoded with the technique in section 4.1.4 of RFC 1035. In this scheme a whole domain name, or the labels at the end of one, is replaced by a pointer to an earlier occurrence of the same name.

The RFC admits this is complex, but DHCP option space is limited and search strings tend to repeat the same domain, so the compression is useful and likely to be effective.

For this option, a pointer refers to an offset within the data portion of the option, not counting the option code byte or the length byte. When several options are present, the offset is within the complete combined block of data.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing the same long address twice, you write it once and later just say see the earlier one.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC encodes the list eng.apple.com. and marketing.apple.com.. The encoding is split across three Domain Search Options, but they are logically one block of data.

The name eng.apple.com. ends with a zero byte, the null root label, as RFC 1035 requires. The name marketing ends with the two-octet pointer C004 (hex), which points to offset 4 in the combined data, where apple.com. already appears.

Every search domain name must end either with a zero or with a two-octet compression pointer. If a receiver reaches the end of the combined data while part-way through a name, without finding either, it MUST discard the partial name as invalid.
sections.eli5: The second name borrows the end of the first name by pointing back to it, like writing see page 4 instead of repeating a paragraph.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attacks on DHCP are covered in RFC 2131 and RFC 3118. With this option, a rogue DHCP server might redirect traffic. A user who types myhost expecting myhost.bigco.com could be sent to myhost.roguedomain.com.

DNSSEC does not stop this, because the records for the rogue name might be legitimately signed. This makes the option a more fruitful target than a fake DNS server option.

To reduce the risk, the RFC recommends that hosts implementing the option SHOULD also follow the search list recommendations in section 6 of RFC 1536. Manually configured DNS parameters SHOULD NOT be overridden by DHCP. Implementations MAY require DHCP authentication before accepting the option.
sections.eli5: A sneaky helper could hand your computer a list of wrong neighborhoods, so you end up at the wrong house. Being careful about whose list you trust helps.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA assigned DHCP option code 119 to the Domain Search Option. The RFC makes no other IANA requests.
sections.eli5: The official list of option numbers now has number 119 reserved for this one.
